title: Neural Control and Coordination
description: Grade 11 Biology: the neuron and nerve impulse, the central and peripheral nervous system, the brain and spinal cord, reflex action, and the sense organs.

topics.title: The Neuron and the Nerve Impulse
topics.concept:
For the body to work as one unit, its many parts must be coordinated — made to work together at the right time. In animals this is done in two ways: rapidly by the nervous system (using electrical signals) and more slowly by the endocrine system (using chemical hormones). This chapter is about neural (nervous) control.

The basic unit of the nervous system is the neuron (nerve cell) — a special cell built to carry messages quickly. A neuron has three parts:

  • The cell body (cyton) — contains the nucleus.
  • Many short branches called dendrites — which receive signals.
  • A long fibre called the axon — which carries the signal away to the next cell.

The message that travels along a neuron is the nerve impulse — an electrical signal. It moves along the axon and reaches the end, where the neuron meets the next neuron (or a muscle). This tiny gap between two neurons is the synapse. At the synapse the electrical signal cannot jump the gap directly, so the neuron releases chemical messengers called neurotransmitters, which carry the signal across to the next neuron. In this way impulses pass from neuron to neuron, always in one direction. A bundle of many axons wrapped together forms a nerve.

examples.problem: Example 1: Name the three parts of a neuron and their functions.
examples.solution:
A neuron has a body and two kinds of branches.

  • Cell body (cyton) — contains the nucleus.
  • Dendrites — receive signals; axon — carries the signal away.
examples.answer: Cell body (nucleus), dendrites (receive signals) and axon (carries the signal away).

examples.solution:
It is the message a neuron carries.

  • A nerve impulse is an electrical signal that travels along a neuron.
examples.answer: A nerve impulse is the electrical signal that travels along a neuron.

examples.problem: Example 3: How does a signal cross the synapse between two neurons?
examples.solution:
The electrical signal cannot jump the gap.

  • The neuron releases chemicals called neurotransmitters.
  • These carry the signal across the synapse to the next neuron.
examples.answer: Chemical messengers called neurotransmitters are released to carry the signal across the synapse.

recap:
• Coordination: fast nervous system (electrical) + slower endocrine system (hormones).
  • Neuron = unit of the nervous system: cell body (nucleus), dendrites (receive), axon (carry away).
  • Nerve impulse = electrical signal; gap between neurons = synapse; crossed by neurotransmitters.
  • A bundle of axons = a nerve.

quiz.q: The basic unit of the nervous system is the:
quiz.explanation: The neuron (nerve cell) is the basic unit of the nervous system.

quiz.q: The gap between two neurons across which signals pass is the:
quiz.explanation: The synapse is the junction between two neurons.

topics.title: The Nervous System: Brain, Spinal Cord and Reflexes
topics.concept:
The human nervous system has two main divisions: the central nervous system (CNS) — the brain and the spinal cord, which process information and give commands — and the peripheral nervous system (PNS) — the network of nerves that connects the CNS to the rest of the body.

The brain is the control centre, protected inside the skull. It has three main parts:

  • Cerebrum — the large, folded front part; the centre of thinking, memory, intelligence, the senses and voluntary actions.
  • Cerebellum — below and behind the cerebrum; controls balance and the coordination of muscular movements.
  • Medulla oblongata (brain stem) — connects to the spinal cord; controls involuntary actions like heartbeat, breathing and digestion.

The spinal cord runs down the back inside the backbone; it carries messages between the brain and the body and controls reflexes.

A reflex action is a quick, automatic response to a stimulus that does not need conscious thought — for example, pulling your hand away from a hot object. The path the signal follows is the reflex arc: a receptor detects the stimulus → a sensory neuron carries the message to the spinal cord → the spinal cord processes it → a motor neuron carries the command to a muscle (effector), which acts. Because the action is decided in the spinal cord (not the brain), it is very fast and protects us from harm.

examples.problem: Example 1: Name the two main divisions of the human nervous system.
examples.solution:
One is central, one peripheral.

  • The central nervous system (brain and spinal cord).
  • The peripheral nervous system (the nerves).
examples.answer: The central nervous system (brain + spinal cord) and the peripheral nervous system (nerves).

examples.problem: Example 2: Which part of the brain controls balance and coordination of movements?
examples.solution:
Recall the brain parts.

  • The cerebellum controls balance and muscular coordination.

examples.problem: Example 3: Trace the reflex arc when you touch a hot object.
examples.solution:
Follow the signal path.

  • Receptor → sensory neuron → spinal cord → motor neuron → muscle (effector).
examples.answer: Receptor → sensory neuron → spinal cord → motor neuron → muscle (effector), which pulls the hand away.

recap:
• CNS = brain + spinal cord; PNS = the nerves.
  • Brain: cerebrum (thinking, senses, voluntary), cerebellum (balance, coordination), medulla (heartbeat, breathing — involuntary).
  • Spinal cord: links brain & body, controls reflexes.
  • Reflex arc: receptor → sensory neuron → spinal cord → motor neuron → effector (fast, automatic).

quiz.q: The part of the brain responsible for thinking and memory is the:
quiz.explanation: The cerebrum is the centre of thinking, memory and voluntary action.

quiz.q: A quick, automatic response not needing conscious thought is a:
quiz.explanation: A reflex action is a fast, automatic response via the reflex arc.

topics.title: The Sense Organs
topics.concept:
To respond to the world, the body must first sense it. Sense organs (receptors) are special structures that detect changes (stimuli) in the surroundings and send signals to the brain. Humans have five main sense organs:

  • Eyes — detect light and let us see. Light enters through the cornea and pupil, is focused by the lens onto the light-sensitive retina at the back, which sends signals through the optic nerve to the brain. The iris controls how much light enters.
  • Ears — detect sound and also help with balance. Sound makes the eardrum vibrate; tiny ear bones pass the vibrations to the inner ear (cochlea), which sends signals to the brain.
  • Nose — detects smell (chemicals in the air) using olfactory receptors.
  • Tongue — detects taste using taste buds that sense sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami.
  • Skin — detects touch, pressure, pain, heat and cold.

Each sense organ has receptors suited to a particular kind of stimulus, and all of them work by converting the stimulus into nerve impulses that travel to the brain, where the sensation is finally "felt" and understood. Caring for the sense organs — for example, protecting the eyes from very bright light and the ears from very loud noise — helps keep them healthy.

examples.solution:
They detect the surroundings.

  • Sense organs (receptors) detect changes (stimuli) in the surroundings.
  • They send signals to the brain.
examples.answer: Sense organs are receptors that detect stimuli in the surroundings and send signals to the brain.

examples.problem: Example 2: Which part of the eye is light-sensitive, and what does it do?
examples.solution:
Light is focused onto the back of the eye.

  • The retina is the light-sensitive layer.
  • It sends signals through the optic nerve to the brain.
examples.answer: The retina; it is light-sensitive and sends signals via the optic nerve to the brain.

examples.problem: Example 3: Name the five sense organs and the stimulus each detects.
examples.solution:
Match each organ to its stimulus.

  • Eyes (light), ears (sound/balance), nose (smell).
  • Tongue (taste), skin (touch/temperature/pain).

recap:
• Sense organs (receptors) detect stimuli and signal the brain.
  • Eyes (light → retina → optic nerve), ears (sound + balance), nose (smell), tongue (taste buds), skin (touch, pressure, pain, temperature).
  • All convert stimuli into nerve impulses sent to the brain, where sensation is felt.
  • Protect eyes (bright light) and ears (loud noise).

quiz.q: The light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye is the:
quiz.explanation: The retina is the light-sensitive layer that signals the brain.
The tongue's taste buds detect taste.

questions.q: Rapid coordination in the body using electrical signals is done by the:
questions.explanation: The nervous system gives fast, electrical coordination.

questions.q: The basic unit of the nervous system is the:
questions.explanation: The neuron is the basic structural and functional unit.

questions.q: The long fibre of a neuron that carries the signal away is the:
questions.explanation: The axon carries the impulse away from the cell body.

questions.q: The message that travels along a neuron is a/an:
questions.explanation: The nerve impulse is an electrical signal.

questions.q: The gap between two neurons is the:
questions.explanation: The synapse is the junction between two neurons.

questions.q: Chemicals that carry the signal across a synapse are:
questions.explanation: Neurotransmitters carry the signal across the synapse.

questions.q: The brain and spinal cord together form the:
questions.explanation: The CNS is the brain plus the spinal cord.

questions.q: The largest, thinking part of the brain is the:
questions.explanation: The cerebrum handles thinking, memory and voluntary action.

questions.q: Balance and coordination of movement are controlled by the:
questions.explanation: The cerebellum controls balance and coordination.

questions.q: Involuntary actions like heartbeat and breathing are controlled by the:
questions.explanation: The medulla oblongata controls involuntary vital actions.

questions.q: A quick automatic response such as pulling the hand from a hot object is a:
questions.explanation: This is a reflex action, processed by the spinal cord.

questions.q: The correct order of the reflex arc is:
options: Receptor → sensory neuron → spinal cord → motor neuron → effector
questions.explanation: The reflex arc runs receptor → sensory → spinal cord → motor → effector.

questions.q: The eye detects:
questions.explanation: The eye is the sense organ for light (sight).

questions.q: The cochlea, important for hearing, is found in the:
questions.explanation: The cochlea is in the inner ear and is used for hearing.

questions.q: Touch, pressure, pain and temperature are detected by the:
questions.explanation: The skin detects touch, pressure, pain and temperature.

questions.q: Impulses pass across a synapse in one direction only because neurotransmitters are released from:
options: One side and received on the other
questions.explanation: Only one neuron releases neurotransmitters and only the next one has receptors, fixing the direction.

questions.q: A reflex action is faster than a normal voluntary action mainly because the decision is made by the:
questions.explanation: Bypassing the brain and using the short spinal pathway makes reflexes very fast and protective.

questions.q: Damage to the cerebellum would most likely affect a person's:
questions.explanation: The cerebellum governs balance and coordination, so its damage disturbs these.

questions.q: Reading a book and then deciding to turn the page is a voluntary action controlled mainly by the:
questions.explanation: Conscious, decided actions are directed by the cerebrum.

questions.q: When you enter a dim room, the pupil widens. This adjustment of light entering the eye is controlled by the:
questions.explanation: The iris changes the size of the pupil to control how much light enters.

questions.q: Constant exposure to very loud noise can harm hearing because it can damage the receptors in the:
questions.explanation: Loud noise damages the delicate sound receptors of the cochlea, reducing hearing.
